title: Direct wildcard engine: correctness and performance
scope: Requested engine rewrite and validation, rather than an exhaustive search for all optimization opportunities. Direct WildcardMatch and preserved WildcardMatchRegex; .NET Standard 2.1/.NET 10/.NET 11 source targets, timed on .NET 10 x64. Continuation: catalogue-driven optimization of committed direct engine 4bc779e; original charts remain historical. New control/candidate charts share a distinct .NET 10 direct-engine epoch. No application throughput claim.
question: Can a direct iterative wildcard engine preserve the Regex contract and improve common complete calls while avoiding per-match buffers? Which additional measured mechanisms improve the committed direct engine?

summary.headline: Direct-engine continuation: complex reused calls 900.1 → 418.3 ns. Original Regex comparisons remain below in their historical epoch; compiled Regex remains workload dependent.

hypotheses.claim: A direct iterative engine improves common complete calls over ordinary Regex
hypotheses.mechanism: Remove translation, Regex lookup/interpreter and exponential star backtracking
hypotheses.prediction: Repeatable lower static time and zero default match buffers
hypotheses.falsification: Differential mismatch or no repeatable caller benefit
hypotheses.change: Replace WildcardMatch with a direct engine; preserve the original class as WildcardMatchRegex and expose both extensions.
hypotheses.maintainability: Additional independently implemented engine and runtime semantic paths require differential validation; no package dependency, unsafe storage, mutable cache, recursion or match buffer.
hypotheses.codeComments: WildcardEngine documents latest-star invariants, newline anchors, culture groups, bulk scans and timeout checkpoints.
hypotheses.result: Simple static calls: 401.2 → 58.1 ns (-85.5%). Default direct matching allocates no buffers. Compiled Regex remains faster for some reused workloads.
hypotheses.decisionRationale: Requested rewrite passes independent/exhaustive/fuzz checks on four runtimes and improves all measured static and ordinary reused cases. Compiled Regex remains available for workloads where specialization wins.
risks: Polynomial worst-case retries remain; the direct engine is not universally faster than compiled Regex.

hypotheses.claim: Bulk fixed literal runs address scalar long-prefix/suffix costs
hypotheses.mechanism: Library search and ordinal bulk comparison
hypotheses.prediction: Lower long-sparse work while preserving '?' and newline semantics
hypotheses.falsification: Boundary mismatch or complete-call regression
hypotheses.change: For case-sensitive patterns of length at least 32, compare literal prefix/suffix runs in bulk before star retries.
hypotheses.maintainability: Safe indexed string operations and one routing guard; no new storage.
hypotheses.codeComments: Adjacent bulk-path comment links this run and explains keeping short patterns scalar.
hypotheses.result: Final long-sparse comparisons and Tier1 library calls support the integrated path. Initial/final build epochs differ, so an isolated numeric effect is not established. Continuation H-012 removes only this routing in the same compiler/target epoch and makes long-sparse calls about twenty times slower.
hypotheses.decisionRationale: Keep as part of the validated H-001 implementation, not as a separately quantified improvement. Initial source/results remain archived. The later controlled ablation resolves the former constituent-effect uncertainty; initial cross-epoch data remains historical.
risks: Length 32 is a routing choice, not a universal optimum; constituent effects are not isolated.

retainedChanges: Direct, iterative prefix/suffix and latest-star matching with constant auxiliary state. No recursive Regex or wildcard engine fallback.

validityThreats: Generic direct matching does not beat every compiled specialization. Reused compiled Regex is faster on some dense, case-insensitive and complex cases; the compiled control is separately displayed.

Common counts are chosen using the slower ordinary Regex engine, so direct blocks can be shorter than 20ms. Equal delegate/loop overhead is included; no empty-loop subtraction or outlier filtering. Interpret small differences cautiously.
Fixed fixtures favor caches and branch prediction; static pattern cardinality is below Regex.CacheSize. No application traffic, cache-churn, contention throughput or cold-process startup claim.
Only .NET 10 x64 is timed. Correctness on .NET 8/9/10/11 does not establish equivalent speed on other runtimes/architectures or future preview releases.
Initial/final compiler and target epochs differ because concurrent authorized work changed package targets. Final ratios are within epoch; the bulk path's isolated numeric effect is inconclusive.

Constant auxiliary memory does not imply linear time: ordinary retries are O(n*m), and Multiline line-start searches can add an input-length factor. Timeout is cooperative and may overshoot within bulk library calls.

Unicode and Regex parser/option rules are runtime-version contracts. .NET 11 AnyNewLine and whitespace-mode vertical tabs were discovered by differential testing; future changes need the same oracle checks.
Failed/withdrawn fixture and build results remain archived. Existing analyzer/style and transitive test-package warnings do not indicate test failures; successful logs remain available.

Identical-code controls show appreciable per-fixture/per-launch variation. Small compiler/branch effects remain inconclusive. Screening is not an acceptance result; retained integration uses longer blocks and all launch/block distributions.

Control and candidate have distinct assembly identities; JIT address/layout and tiering can differ even for identical source. No hardware branch-miss or cache-miss inference is made from timing alone.

The original thirteen cases have equal importance; ten additional adversarial distributions are explicit contrasts, not an application frequency model. A targeted improvement does not establish improvement on every pattern.

Desktop/uncoordinated background processes are not controlled by the advisory lock. The full raw distributions are retained; no outlier exclusions, overhead subtraction or hidden baseline-epoch comparison.
